title: TrustMod-SM: A Multi-Axis Benchmark for Evaluating Trustworthiness of LLMs in Social Media Content Moderation
claim: A benchmark evaluates systems along several complementary axes, each defined by tailored sub-criteria and metrics, applied across a model suite.
layout: Central hub with five axis cards, detail panels around it, model-scale strip below
description: A hub-and-spoke diagram. A central circle holds a robot mascot with a shield and checkmark. A dashed ring around it carries five small colored cards: Trustfulness (blue), Safety (red), Robustness (green), Fairness (yellow), and Context Integrity (purple). Each card poses a guiding question. Arrows lead from the cards to larger detail panels in the matching colors around the edges. The panels list sub-tasks, metrics and examples. These include label accuracy and ECE, concealment and exaggeration attacks, leetspeak and punctuation perturbations, demographic groups, and stereotype and reclaimed-language cases. A white box along the bottom groups the evaluated models into Lightweight, Prosumer and High-Capacity tiers, with model-family logos. A title and subtitle sit at the top. The eye goes first to the mascot, then to the colored panels.
caption: TrustMod-SM provides a unified evaluation of LLM trustworthiness in social media content moderation with five evaluation axes: trustfulness, fairness, safety, robustness, and context integrity; each with tailored metrics applied to open-weight models.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) show strong potential for social media content moderation, but their trustworthiness beyond overall accuracy remains underexplored. We introduce TrustMod-SM, a benchmark of roughly 29,000 instances across eight datasets, to evaluate LLM moderators on five dimensions: trustfulness, fairness, safety, robustness, and context integrity. Evaluating 16 open-weight models (0.5B-284B parameters, spanning text-only and vision-language architectures) and one closed frontier model, we find persistent trustworthiness gaps. Higher detection accuracy often coincides with greater demographic disparity, and models frequently comply with concealment or exaggeration prompts, assign high confidence to wrong predictions, rarely escalate ambiguous cases, and struggle to separate hate speech from counter-speech or reclaimed language (especially below 8B parameters). Scaling does not uniformly resolve these issues, and no single model excels across all five dimensions.
